title: Candlemas (2 February)
hookLine: forty days after Christmas: Simeon's light, and candles blessed
carry: a light to lighten the gentiles

cards: Two small birds. That's the offering a young couple bring to the temple in Jerusalem, along with their baby.
The law in Leviticus says that after the birth of a son the mother waits seven days, then thirty-three more, and then brings a lamb, or, if she can't afford one, two turtledoves or two young pigeons.
Mary and Joseph come with the birds. In the crowded courts, one man has been waiting for something only he knows about.
Churches keep this day in early February, counting from Christmas, and in some churches it begins with candles. Today's word is what the couple came to do.

teach.h: TO PRESENT HIM TO THE LORD.
teach.b: Luke tells it in the King James Bible: "And when the days of her purification according to the law of Moses were accomplished, they brought him to Jerusalem, to present him to the Lord."
That's the Presentation: a firstborn son brought to the temple and offered back to God, as the law asks. Then Simeon.
Luke says he was just and devout, and that the Holy Ghost had shown him he would not see death before he had seen the Lord's Christ.
So he has been waiting, scanning faces. When this couple with their two birds walks in, he knows.

teach.h: NOW LETTEST THOU THY SERVANT DEPART.
teach.b: He takes the baby in his arms, blesses God, and says words some churches still sing at the close of the day: "Lord, now lettest thou thy servant depart in peace, according to thy word: For mine eyes have seen thy salvation, Which thou hast prepared before the face of all people; A light to lighten the Gentiles, and the glory of thy people Israel."
Simeon is holding a baby who hasn't said a word, and he calls him light, for his own people and for everyone outside them. Light is at the heart of the day's English name, Candlemas.

In some churches candles are blessed and carried in procession against the February dark, in some places the candles for the year ahead. Orthodox Christians call the feast the Meeting, because Simeon and the child meet.
Catholics and Anglicans often call it the Presentation. Simeon's part ends with a man at peace, ready to go, because he got to hold the light.

how: At Candlemas, Catholic, Anglican and some Lutheran churches bless candles and carry them in procession; Orthodox churches keep the same feast as the Meeting of the Lord, and Simeon's song is sung at evening prayer in several traditions.

games.q: you're Simeon. you've been told you won't die before you see the Christ. a poor couple walks into the temple carrying a baby and two birds. what do you do?
o: wait for someone grander to arrive.
take the baby in your arms and bless God.
ask the priests whether this could be the one.
games.why: Simeon took him up in his arms and blessed God: "Lord, now lettest thou thy servant depart in peace." he recognized the light in a family who had come with the birds.

practice: Light a candle, or switch on one small lamp in a dim room, and look at it. Think of something you've waited a long time to see, and whether it came.
If you pray, say Simeon's words slowly, Lord, now lettest thou thy servant depart in peace; if not, let your shoulders drop, like someone whose long wait is over.
